value.overview: The Nazca Booby (Sula granti) is a large tropical seabird of the eastern Pacific Ocean. It is closely related to the Masked Booby but is recognized as a separate species. Nazca Boobies spend most of their lives at sea, returning to isolated oceanic islands to breed in dense colonies. They are powerful fliers and plunge-divers that feed mainly on fish and squid captured in offshore waters.
value.classification: The Nazca Booby belongs to the booby and gannet family Sulidae, within the order Suliformes. It was formerly treated as a subspecies of the Masked Booby but is now recognized as a distinct species.
value.identification: Adults are large seabirds with a mostly white body, dark brown to black wings and tail, and a conspicuous black facial mask around the eyes and bill. The long, pointed bill is usually orange, pinkish, or yellowish, while the feet are gray. Immature birds are browner overall and develop adult plumage gradually. In Costa Rica, careful identification is important because Nazca Boobies can resemble Masked, Cocos, and Blue-footed Boobies.
value.rangeHabitat: The species is distributed across the tropical eastern Pacific, breeding on isolated islands including the Galápagos, Malpelo, Clipperton, and Cocos Island. In Costa Rica, it is a breeding seabird of Isla del Coco and nearby rocky islets, where it uses open ground and cliff-top or coastal nesting sites. It also forages widely in offshore Pacific waters. Individuals have occasionally been recorded in waters off the mainland and, rarely, in the Caribbean side of Costa Rica.
value.migrationStatus: The Nazca Booby is not a regular long-distance migrant. Adults generally remain associated with breeding islands and nearby oceanic waters, while juveniles and nonbreeding birds disperse more widely. In Costa Rica, it is resident at Isla del Coco but can occur irregularly offshore, with occasional vagrant records beyond the Pacific, including Caribbean waters.
value.breeding: Nazca Boobies breed colonially on remote tropical islands, usually in open, sparsely vegetated terrain. They defend small territories around a nest made from loose vegetation, soil, and other available material. The female normally lays one egg, and both parents share incubation and care of the chick. Breeding timing varies among colonies and may be influenced by food availability. Colonies on Cocos Island form part of the species' small Central American breeding range.
value.dietFeeding: The diet consists mainly of small to medium-sized marine fish, along with squid and other available oceanic prey. Nazca Boobies usually forage offshore, often several kilometers from breeding colonies. They locate prey from the air and dive steeply into the water, sometimes entering at high speed from considerable height. Adults may also take advantage of tuna and other predatory fish that drive schooling prey toward the surface.
value.behavior: Nazca Boobies are highly aerial seabirds that spend much of the day soaring, traveling, and searching for prey over open ocean. They are strongly colonial during breeding but defend space around their nests with displays, calls, bill movements, and aggressive postures. At sea they may forage alone or in loose groups, particularly where large predatory fish concentrate prey. Young birds disperse widely after fledging before returning to breeding areas.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered to be decreasing, although the species remains widely distributed and locally abundant at several major colonies.
